reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 18-1] Estimating the cost of drilled shaft foundations is Step 15 of the overall design and construction process of Chapter 8 (Figure 8-1). In planning, the design engineer's preliminary estimates compare drilled shafts with other technically feasible foundation systems and may be one factor in selecting the foundation type; in final design, the engineer's estimate supports total project cost before bid. The actual cost is set in the open marketplace by competitive bidding. Unless drilled shafts have a clear advantage (cost, environmental factors, site constraints, etc.), the best way to obtain the lowest overall foundation cost for a highway project is to design competing foundation systems and request bids on each; the added engineering effort is often more than offset by the savings. The chapter briefly addresses factors that impact cost and gives general guidance on estimating.
key_points: Cost estimation is Step 15 of the Chapter 8 process
Preliminary estimates compare foundation types; final estimates support pre-bid project cost
Design competing foundation systems and bid each; extra design effort is often offset by savings
sections.applicability: Cost estimation for drilled shaft foundations; alternative foundation comparison

sections.title: Factors Influencing Cost
sections.body: [pp. 18-1 to 18-4] Cost varies widely with location and time, and with the quality and detail of subsurface data and the contractor's assumed construction method. Factors: subsurface and site conditions, probably the largest influence (rock hardness; trafficability, nearby structures, traffic control, utilities, overhead lines or decks, trees, contours, cut-off elevation relative to ground; access and time restrictions such as night work and lane closures; low-headroom rigs cost approximately three times rigs operating in the open, need field splices of casing and cage, and normally leave permanent casing); shaft geometry (deeper costs more per unit; in soil the unit cost per volume falls with diameter until holes exceed what readily available equipment can drill, typically larger than about 8-ft diameter; larger holes become increasingly difficult in hard rock); number of shafts (more shafts, lower unit cost); specifications and inspection (unneeded permanent casing, a 'tough' inspector, classified versus unclassified excavation, NDT/NDE requirements especially with penalties for negative results, and a 'method spec' drive up pricing; Chapter 14, Appendix D); obstructions (no-obstruction-pay projects get large contingencies, man-made-only medium, full cost reimbursement low); weather; work time restrictions; travel and living costs (e.g., Alaska, Hawaii); schedule and penalty clauses; work rules (oilers, certified welders, union or non-union, prevailing wage); governmental regulations; availability of optimum equipment; availability and cost of concrete; contractor experience and ingenuity; material costs (e.g., steel); economic conditions; insurance and bonding; cost of money and payment terms; contract terms (contractor assuming all risks, including differing site conditions); general contractor's fees, and whether the general contractor supplies concrete or cages (drilled shaft contractors prefer sole responsibility for quality control). A 1997 contractor survey (O'Neill and Reese, 1999; 50 shafts in three scenarios; prices no longer valid) concluded: hard rock sockets cost about three times, on average, a shaft through dry overburden above rock; wet bouldery alluvium overburden over a soft geomaterial socket costs about twice per unit length the soft socket; drilling slurry or full-length casing is about one-third more expensive than dry, stable overburden; the most uncertain cost is excavating hard rock.
key_points: Subsurface and site conditions probably the largest cost influence
Low-headroom rigs cost approximately three times open rigs; permanent casing is the norm
Soil drilling unit cost per volume falls with diameter up to about 8 ft
Method specs, NDT penalties and unneeded permanent casing drive up pricing
Obstruction pay: none = large contingency, man-made only = medium, all reimbursed = low
1997 survey: hard rock socket about 3x dry overburden; slurry or full casing about 1/3 more
sections.applicability: Preliminary and final cost estimates; specification writing to reduce contingencies

sections.title: Commentary
sections.body: [p. 18-4] With so many variables there is no single formula or method giving highly accurate costs for a specific project before bidding. Contractors estimate from time and materials; local historical cost information from awarded contracts can guide reasonable preliminary estimates for comparing foundation types, and for final pre-bid estimates historical prices combined with experience and knowledge of constructability are the basis. Whatever the foundation's share of project cost, the prudent action is to select a contractor with the necessary equipment, experienced personnel and a record of high-quality construction; some agencies require drilled shaft contractor prequalification.
key_points: No single formula gives accurate pre-bid costs
Historical awarded-contract prices guide preliminary estimates; add constructability knowledge for final estimates
Select a capable contractor; some agencies prequalify drilled shaft contractors

sections.title: Publicly Available Price Data
sections.body: [pp. 18-4 to 18-7] Most state transportation agencies keep databases of submitted bid prices ('bid tabs') on websites, giving a snapshot of actual costs by state and sometimes region. Table 18-1 is a TxDOT statewide low-bid summary (TxDOT uses many shafts in a competitive market); geology and shaft lengths (not tabulated) varied widely, so such tables cannot pinpoint costs for a particular project, but they show costs relative to diameter and, comparing latest bids with the 12-month moving average, pricing trends in Texas; they should not be considered reliable for other regions. Table 18-2: bids by six contractors (numbered lowest to highest total project bid) and the Engineer's Estimate for one Galveston, TX project: wide ranges for some sizes, and the winning bidder did not necessarily have the lowest shaft prices; shafts were about 4 percent of the winning bid on a 5-mile interstate project. Table 18-3 (California, 2017) shows subsurface effects: 24-inch rock sockets averaged $390 per ft (two projects), about 1.75 times 24-inch shafts in soil at $223 per ft (six projects); a single 72-inch project ($1,518 per ft) exceeded a single 96-inch project ($1,462 per ft), so other factors controlled; seismic reinforcing amounts are not identified in bid tabs. Know what each bid item includes: some states separate excavation and concrete; permanent casing, mobilization and load testing are typically separate; site preparation, traffic control and cap concrete are outside shaft items but affect total cost. The heading prints 'PUBLICALLY'.
key_points: State DOT bid tabs give snapshots of actual costs; not transferable to other regions
Table 18-1: TxDOT statewide low bids by diameter, month ending 5/31/2018 and 12-month moving average
Table 18-2: one Galveston project, six bidders vs. Engineer's Estimate; wide price ranges
Table 18-3: Caltrans 2017; 24-in. rock socket $390/ft about 1.75 times 24-in. soil shaft $223/ft
Check what each bid item includes (excavation, concrete, casing, mobilization, load tests)

sections.title: Contractors' Cost Computation
sections.body: [pp. 18-8 to 18-9] A drilled shaft bid has variable costs (functions of quantities of concrete, steel, excavation, etc.), costs unique to each project but viewed as fixed (engineering, bonding, moving equipment), and overhead (ongoing costs of running the company). The Drilled Shaft Contractor examines the contract documents (geotechnical reports, boring logs, drawings, specifications), appraises the site on a visit, sets a tentative work plan (methods, equipment, manpower), makes a quantity takeoff (concrete, steel, NDT testing, slurry, other materials), then a rough schedule after careful review of specifications that affect it (e.g., restrictions on drilling adjacent to recently poured shafts, time waiting for NDT and approval by the resident engineer).
key_points: Bid components: variable costs, jobsite fixed costs, overhead
Sequence: contract documents, site visit, work plan, quantity takeoff, rough schedule
Schedule affected by adjacent-shaft drilling restrictions and NDT approval waits
sections.applicability: Understanding contractor cost structure; owner estimate preparation

sections.title: Variable Costs
sections.body: [p. 18-9] Labor: from the rough schedule, including fringe benefits, payroll taxes, anticipated overtime and possibly unproductive time from weather or other causes (see Contingencies). Materials: priced from suppliers, including overruns and waste such as concrete overpour and overbreak; reinforcing steel and NDT testing usually through subcontractors or suppliers; NDT tubes may be tied in by the contractor or supplied by the rebar supplier, and the estimator must know where the item is carried. Rented equipment: from supplier quotations and the schedule. Contractor-owned equipment: some contractors keep databases of owning and running costs (capital cost, financing, insurance, depreciation, major repairs, wear parts, FOG - fuel, oil, grease - and others), estimate annual operating hours, and set hourly charges collected in an Equipment Costing account; others use published rates (Dataquest, Blue Book, State Force-Account rates); others carry only FOG as variable and put other equipment costs in Overhead. Equipment costs are then calculated from equipment hours, like labor.
key_points: Labor from the schedule, with overtime and weather allowances
Materials include overpour and overbreak; know where NDT tubes are carried
Owned equipment: hourly rates from owning and operating costs, published rates, or FOG only
sections.applicability: Contractor variable costs for drilled shaft bids

sections.title: Jobsite Fixed Costs
sections.body: [p. 18-10] A separate estimate covers moves to and from the site, moving rigs between foundation locations (possibly significant offshore), site trailers etc., bonding, engineering, supervision (some carry it as variable), project management (some carry it in Overhead) and other fixed costs.
key_points: Jobsite fixed costs: moves, rig moves between locations, trailers, bonding, engineering, supervision, management
sections.applicability: Contractor jobsite fixed costs for drilled shaft bids

sections.title: Overhead
sections.body: [p. 18-10] The cost of running the corporation is written off over the year's work, as a percentage of total job costs, a daily charge against major equipment, or within markup. It may include management salaries and benefits, administration (payroll, AR, AP), telephones and IT, over- or under-runs in the equipment costing account, professional fees, insurance, R&D, office rent, yard expenses, equipment costs not charged to projects, and others.
key_points: Overhead recovered as percentage of job cost, daily equipment charge, or in markup
sections.applicability: Contractor overhead in drilled shaft bids

sections.title: Contingencies
sections.body: [p. 18-10] Some contractors estimate contingencies separately, others cover them in markup: inclement weather, labor disruption, repair of anomalies, unit prices for materials, delays from equipment repairs and maintenance, schedule disruption by others, potential differing site condition (DSC) claims that may be difficult to collect, potential Liquidated Damages, and others.
key_points: Contingencies: weather, labor, anomaly repair, material prices, equipment delays, DSC claims, liquidated damages
sections.applicability: Contractor contingencies in drilled shaft bids

sections.title: Markup
sections.body: [p. 18-11] Some contractors add one percentage markup to total cost; others mark up cost types differently by uncertainty (labor traditionally much more volatile than subcontractor costs). Reasonable markups cannot be quoted without knowing where a contractor's costs are carried and whether markup includes some of them or is only gross profit. Markup varies with market forces, backlog, and comfort with the type and location of work and the client's track record.
key_points: Markup may be single or by cost type (labor more volatile than subcontracts)
Reasonable markups cannot be quoted without knowing where costs are carried
sections.applicability: Contractor markup in drilled shaft bids

sections.title: Unit Prices
sections.body: [p. 18-11] The total bid is assigned to owner-designated bid items, some unit priced and some fixed or lump sum. The contractor appraises how volatile quantities may be (shaft lengths, casing) and decides how much cost to spread across unit priced items versus lump sum items such as Mobilization and Engineering; this is risky, and even a good estimate can lose money if costs are spread unfavorably relative to final quantities.
key_points: Spreading cost between unit-price and lump-sum items is a risky judgment on quantity volatility
sections.applicability: Allocation of drilled shaft costs to unit-price and lump-sum bid items

sections.title: Other Considerations
sections.body: [p. 18-11] When comparing unit prices, know what is and is not included: concrete, reinforcing steel, permanent casing, load testing, NDT testing and others may be in the drilled shaft contract or supplied by the general contractor or others.
key_points: Compare unit prices only with clear knowledge of included items

sections.title: Typical Cost Estimating Template
sections.body: [pp. 18-11 to 18-13] Figure 18-1 is a Florida DOT bridge cost estimating template (Structures Design Guidelines, July 2004, 9.2 BDR Bridge Cost Estimating) with a 3-step procedure: Step 1 estimates substructure (including drilled shafts) and superstructure component costs from historical bid tab data; Step 2 adjusts for site variables (rural -6 percent, urban counties +6 percent, over water +3 percent, phased construction +20 percent premium on affected units); Step 3 is a 'reality check' against historic cost per square foot for similar bridge types, with justification if outside the range. Drilled shaft total in-place cost per LF in the template for 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 ft: on land with casing salvaged $239, $277, $340, $441, $542 (8 and 9 ft not given); in water with casing salvaged $277, $302, $353, $479, $605, $806 (9 ft not given); in water with permanent casing $428, $466, $554, $643, $781, $970, $1184. Some superstructure steps are omitted, and some template costs are outdated; it illustrates how an agency estimates for budgeting and comparison with bids.
key_points: FDOT template: Step 1 unit costs, Step 2 site adjustments, Step 3 cost per square foot check
Step 2: rural -6%, urban +6%, over water +3%, phased +20% on affected units
Drilled shaft in-place cost per LF by diameter and casing condition (2004 values, some outdated)
figures: Figure 18-1: Example Cost Estimating Template (Source: Florida DOT)
sections.applicability: Agency cost estimating template for drilled shafts

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: [p. 18-13] Site conditions, both subsurface and surface, often are the most significant cost factors. Cost data from recent projects are a valuable tool for engineering estimates, but drilled shaft costs can be highly project-specific and there is no single reliable method of predicting actual costs. Knowing how contractors prepare bids helps engineers estimate for planning and compare foundation options.
key_points: Site conditions often most significant cost factor
Recent project cost data valuable, but costs are project-specific; no single reliable prediction method
Understanding contractor bid preparation helps engineers' estimates
